lesson.title: English's Fossil Umlauts
lesson.subtitle: man/men, foot/feet, goose/geese, mouse/mice — mapped onto German pairs

hook.title: Your Fossil Collection
hook.content: English keeps exactly seven or so living umlaut plurals, and they are the oldest words in the language: man/men, foot/feet, goose/geese, mouse/mice, tooth/teeth, woman/women, louse/lice. German keeps the same system productive: Mann/Männer, Fuß/Füße, Maus/Mäuse, Zahn/Zähne, Stadt/Städte. Pair them up and the correspondence is total: the same vowel-pull, one shore writing dots, the other just changing the letter. This lesson is a museum tour of your own fossils, displayed beside their living German relatives.

footnotes.title: The Museum's Oldest Piece
footnotes.content: foot/feet and Fuß/Füße are the showpiece: the u was pulled to ü/ee by the same ancient -iz plural, and both languages kept the pulled vowel. The plural of foot has been irregular for 2,000 years in two languages — consistency across the North Sea.

pattern.title: The Display Cases
pattern.content: Case one: man/men ↔ Mann/Männer — the a pulled forward. Case two: foot/feet ↔ Fuß/Füße. Case three: mouse/mice ↔ Maus/Mäuse. Case four: tooth/teeth ↔ Zahn/Zähne (hinted: the t→z twin you own from the sibilant family). Case five: goose/geese ↔ Gans/Gänse (hint: the gans family). Case six, the broken pair: child/children ↔ Kind/Kinder — English went even MORE irregular (the old plural -r survives in children!), German stayed regular. Case seven: house/houses ↔ Haus/Häuser — English took the regular exit; German kept the umlaut. Every case is one law: the vanished i pulled, the languages kept different evidence.
pattern.linguist_note: The -r plural in 'children' is the same -r suffix German uses in Kinder, Bücher, Männer — English's children is a double plural, -r plus -en, the only place the Germanic -r plural survives in English spelling.

exercises.prompt: The display cases — match each English fossil with its living German pair:
exercises.target_answer: Mann / Männer, Fuß / Füße, Maus / Mäuse, Tochter / Töchter, Vogel / Vögel, Kuh / Kühe
exercises.explanation: Same vowel-pull, same words — the dots in German are the only visible difference. Kine, English's own umlaut plural of cow, survived into the 1800s.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'children' end in -en while German says 'Kinder'?
options: German dropped an -en that was always there
children is a DOUBLE plural — the Germanic -r plus -en; Kinder keeps the -r alone
exercises.target_answer: children is a DOUBLE plural — the Germanic -r plus -en; Kinder keeps the -r alone
exercises.meaning: children ↔ Kinder: the same -r plural fossil
exercises.explanation: child + -er + -en: the only place English still shows the Germanic -r plural that German uses productively. The feminine -n drawer is full too: Rechnung → Rechnungen, Blume → Blumen, Lampe → Lampen, Bluse → Blusen — no umlaut, just the -n.

exercises.prompt: Which pair shows English TAKING the regular exit where German kept umlaut?
exercises.meaning: Haus/Häuser kept the dots; house/houses regularized
exercises.explanation: English regularized most nouns with -s; only the oldest words kept their umlaut. Haus never surrendered. The new nouns sort themselves: Blatt → Blätter (umlaut -er), Auge → Augen (-n), Ei → Eier (-er), Knie → Knie (zero) — four nouns, four drawers.

exercises.prompt: What English pair is the fossil twin of 'Fuß/Füße'?
exercises.explanation: The u-pull happened once, in Proto-Germanic, before the languages split — both kept the result forever.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The men have big feet' (die Füße)

vocab_hints.note: groß gains -e before plural nouns — the adjective waves the umlaut flag too

exercises.explanation: Two umlaut plurals plus an adjective ending — the fossil museum in one sentence.

summary.outcome: Map every English fossil umlaut onto its German pair and use the plurals in sentences.
summary.takeaway: man/men, foot/feet, mouse/mice — the same i-mutation as Mann/Männer, Fuß/Füße, Maus/Mäuse. One law, two spellings.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the five plural patterns — sort twenty-five nouns into their plural classes.

mann.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *mann- — the identical twin of man; German keeps the short a English lengthened. [wiktionary]

tochter.context_phrase: Meine Tochter lernt in der Schule.
tochter.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and gh → ch.

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

vogel.context_translation: The bird sings in the garden.
vogel.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fuglaz, likely from 'to fly' — cognate with English fowl. [wiktionary]

kuh.context_phrase: Die Kuh steht auf der Weide.
kuh.context_translation: The cow stands in the meadow.
kuh.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kōz, PIE *gʷṓws — the twin of English cow. [wiktionary]

blatt.context_translation: The leaf falls from the tree.
blatt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *bladą 'leaf' — English blade is the same word, meanings split. [wiktionary]

ei.context_phrase: Ich esse ein Ei zum Frühstück.
ei.context_translation: I eat an egg for breakfast.
ei.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *aij — Wiktionary lists English ey and egg as cognates. [wiktionary]

knie.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *knewą — the identical twin of English knee (silent k in both). [wiktionary]

rechnung.etymology_derivation: rechnen + -ung — the twin of English reckoning; the entry lists English reckoning as a cognate. [wiktionary]

blume.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *blōmō 'blossom'; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

lampe.context_phrase: Die Lampe steht auf dem Tisch.
lampe.context_translation: The lamp is on the table.
lampe.etymology_derivation: From Latin lampada — the same Latin loan as English lamp. [wiktionary]

bluse.context_phrase: Die Bluse ist weiß und die Hose ist schwarz.
bluse.context_translation: The blouse is white and the trousers are black.
bluse.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French blouse - the same French word that gave English blouse. [wiktionary]
